## Proof

We wish to determine when $\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^n}|f(\|k\|)|$ converges absolutely, given $f(x)=O(x^{-p})$ as $x\to+\infty$.

**Reduction to a lattice sum.** Since $f(x)=O(x^{-p})$, there exist $C>0$ and $R_0>0$ such that $|f(x)|\le C\,x^{-p}$ for all $x\ge R_0$. The set $\{k\in\mathbb{Z}^n:\|k\|<R_0\}$ is finite, so it contributes only a finite amount to the sum. Hence absolute convergence is equivalent to the convergence of

$$\sum_{\substack{k\in\mathbb{Z}^n\\ \|k\|\ge R_0}} \|k\|^{-p}.$$

**Counting lattice points by radius.** Let $N(R)=\#\{k\in\mathbb{Z}^n:\|k\|\le R\}$. A standard volume comparison gives $N(R)=O(R^n)$: indeed each lattice point is the center of a unit cube contained in the ball of radius $R+\sqrt n$, so $N(R)\le (2(R+\sqrt n)+1)^n=O(R^n)$, and conversely the ball of radius $R-\sqrt n$ is covered, giving $N(R)\ge cR^n$ for large $R$, so in fact $N(R)\asymp R^n$.

Define the shell count $a_m=N(m+1)-N(m)=\#\{k:\|k\|\in(m,m+1]\}$. Since $N(R)\asymp R^n$, we have $a_m\asymp m^{n-1}$ (the derivative of $R^n$). More precisely, $a_m=O(m^{n-1})$ and $a_m\ge c\,m^{n-1}$ for $m$ large.

**Integral test via shells.** For $\|k\|\in(m,m+1]$ we have $\|k\|^{-p}\asymp m^{-p}$ (up to constants independent of $m$). Therefore

$$\sum_{\substack{k\in\mathbb{Z}^n\\\|k\|\ge R_0}}\|k\|^{-p}\asymp \sum_{m\ge \lfloor R_0\rfloor} a_m\,m^{-p}\asymp \sum_{m\ge M} m^{n-1}\cdot m^{-p}=\sum_{m\ge M} m^{n-1-p}.$$

The series $\sum m^{n-1-p}$ is a $p$-series with exponent $n-1-p$; it converges if and only if

$$n-1-p<-1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p>n.$$

**Conclusion.** The original sum converges absolutely if and only if $p>n$.

- If $p>n$: the bound $|f(x)|\le Cx^{-p}$ and the shell estimate above give $\sum|f(\|k\|)|\le \text{const}+\sum m^{n-1-p}<\infty$.
- If $p\le n$: taking $f(x)=x^{-p}$ (which is $O(x^{-p})$) yields $\sum\|k\|^{-p}\asymp\sum m^{n-1-p}=\infty$, so absolute convergence fails in general.

Hence the necessary and sufficient condition is

$$\boxed{p>n.}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
